title: Dining Hall
summary: Navigate the messy reality of a crowded dining hall. Multiple paths to success—and multiple ways to interpret what success even means.

nodes.text:
You push through the heavy doors. The dining hall hits you all at once—clattering trays, conversations layered over each other, clusters of people who all seem to know exactly where they belong.

Your chest tightens. That familiar thought: everyone is watching. They're not. Probably. But your body doesn't believe that yet.

You see the food line. A table with one person reading, headphones in. A bigger table with a group mid-conversation. An empty corner table. The exit behind you.

You take a breath. Not deep—that would feel weird—just enough to steady yourself. You move toward the food line.

Standing there, you're hyper-aware of everything. The person behind you is too close. Or normal close? The menu board is confusing. Someone ahead is taking forever.

Your mind is loud. Part of you wants to leave. Part of you knows that leaving would make tomorrow harder.

You pause just inside the door, scanning the room like you're looking for someone. Classic move. Buys you time.

The group table has an empty chair. The reading person hasn't looked up. The corner table is safe. The food line is moving.

No one has noticed you yet. You could still leave without it meaning anything.

You pull out your phone before you've even fully entered. It's automatic—something to hold, something to look at. You're not really reading anything.

You drift toward the food line, eyes on the screen. The anxiety dulls slightly. But you feel a little more hidden, a little less present.

You turn and walk out. The relief is instant—the noise fades, the pressure lifts. You're outside before you've really decided.

An hour later, you're still hungry. The dining hall is still open. There's a window of time where you could try again. Or not.

You have your tray. The food is fine. Now comes the real part.

Three options: the empty corner table—safe, solitary. The table with one person reading—lower stakes, but still someone. The group table with the open seat—highest exposure.

Your hands are slightly damp on the tray. You need to decide.

You walk toward the person reading. They have headphones in, a textbook open, a half-eaten sandwich. They don't look up as you approach.

You stop near the empty chair across from them. They still haven't noticed you. You could just sit. Or you could say something.

You sit down without a word. They glance up briefly, register that someone sat down, then go back to their book. No acknowledgment. No hostility. Just... neutral.

You eat. They read. The silence is strange at first—is this awkward? Are you supposed to say something? But after a few minutes, it starts to feel almost comfortable. Two people sharing a table, neither one needing anything from the other.

Your meal is nearly done.

"Is this seat taken?"

They pull out one earbud. "Oh—no, go ahead." They put the earbud back in.

That's it. Four words. You sit down.

They don't seem annoyed. They don't seem happy. They're just... continuing what they were doing. The interaction was so small it barely registered for them.

You eat. They read. The silence settles.

Here's what your brain wants to do: analyze the earbud thing. Did they put it back in too fast? Were they annoyed? Should you have said something else?

But there's another option: accept that it was nothing. A small, neutral moment. Not a rejection. Not a welcome. Just normal.

You walk toward the group table. There are four people, mid-conversation about something—a class, a professor, you're not sure. The empty chair is at the end.

You stop. Heart pounding. The conversation doesn't pause. They haven't noticed you yet.

You could ask. You could just sit. You could stand here another three seconds and feel like an idiot.

"Hey—is this seat taken?"

The nearest person glances up. "Nope, go ahead."

They return to the conversation. It doesn't include you. You sit down.

The interaction was three seconds. Their response was flat—not warm, not cold. Your brain is already trying to decide what that meant.

You decide: that was normal. Not a welcome party. Not a rejection. Just a brief, ordinary moment between strangers.

You eat. The conversation continues around you. Occasionally someone laughs. You're not part of it, but you're also not excluded. You're just... there.

Then there's a lull. One of them turns slightly in your direction.

Your brain latches on: their tone was flat. They barely looked at you. They went right back to their conversation. They didn't want you there.

**[Interpretation: You turned a neutral moment into evidence of rejection]**

You sit down anyway, but the meal already feels wrong. Every laugh that isn't directed at you feels like confirmation. You eat quickly.

They said yes, but they had to. Social obligation. They probably looked at you and thought: here comes the awkward loner.

**[Interpretation: You assumed their compliance was pity, not neutrality]**

You sit, but you're already preparing to leave as soon as it's not weird. The meal is a formality now.

"How's your day going?"

The person nearest you looks up. Brief surprise, then: "Pretty good, thanks. You?"

"Not bad."

They nod. Small smile. The conversation doesn't continue, but it wasn't supposed to. It was just a moment of ordinary human acknowledgment.

You go back to eating. So do they.

The lull passes. The conversation picks back up without you. That's fine. You didn't need to speak. You're here. You're eating. That's enough.

A few more minutes pass. Your meal is almost done.

The small talk is over. Now what?

Your brain has options: replay the exchange critically, looking for where you sounded weird. Or just... let it exist as the neutral thing it was.

The meal is nearly done. Soon you'll leave.

There's a silence. It stretches. Someone checks their phone. Someone else stares at their food.

You're aware of every second. This is the part social anxiety makes hard—sitting in a moment that isn't going anywhere, without escaping or filling it.

The silence isn't hostile. It's just empty. But your body is telling you to leave.

You don't fill the silence. You don't check your phone. You just sit with it.

Thirty seconds. Forty-five. Then someone says something and the conversation resumes. It wasn't about you. It wasn't because of you. It was just a pause.

**[You tolerated discomfort without escaping]**

Your meal is done. Time to leave.

You take the corner table. It's quieter here. No one to navigate, no questions to ask. You eat your meal with your headphones in, eyes mostly down.

The anxiety is manageable. But as you finish, you notice the group table laughing about something. The reader turns a page. Life is happening around you.

You stayed. That counts for something. But part of you wonders what would have happened if you'd sat somewhere else.

Wait.

You notice what your brain is doing. You're making up a story about what they think. You don't actually know. Their flat response could mean anything—tired, distracted, just not expressive. It probably meant nothing.

**[You caught the mind-reading pattern mid-spiral]**

You take a breath. You're still here. You can stay.

You stay. The meal continues. The group talks around you. Occasionally there's a lull, and you sit with it.

It's not comfortable. But it's also not the disaster your brain predicted. You finish eating.

This wasn't a triumphant social success. It was something smaller and maybe more important: you stayed when every instinct told you to leave.

You're back. The dining hall looks the same. The anxiety is still there, but different now—tempered by the knowledge that you already left once and it didn't help.

This time you're doing it on purpose. That changes something.

You're walking out of the dining hall. The meal is over. The interaction is done.

Now your brain gets to decide what that experience meant.

Was it evidence that you can handle ordinary social moments? Or is it already being processed into a list of things you did wrong?

You're done. You gather your things. The person reading hasn't looked up again. You're not sure they'd recognize you if they saw you tomorrow.

But you stayed. You ate your meal in a public space, near another person, without collapsing. That's data.

They respond briefly—"Yeah, just reviewing for a test"—and turn back to their book. The conversation dies immediately.

You eat in silence. It's not hostile, but it's also not comfortable. You pushed when they weren't looking for connection, and now you're both sitting in the aftermath of that mismatch.

Your brain is building a story. They put the earbud back in too fast. Their response was too short. They probably wish you weren't here.

You're eating, but you're not really present. Part of you is already rehearsing how to leave without it being weird.

You sit down without asking. No one says anything. No one looks at you. The conversation continues around you.

Did they notice? Did they care? You can't tell. The ambiguity hangs there as you start eating.

You're standing at the edge of the table, tray in hands, not quite sitting, not quite leaving. Someone glances up briefly, then looks away.

The moment stretches. Every second feels like evidence that you're doing this wrong.

You pull out your phone and scroll. The lull passes without you being part of it. When you look up, the conversation has moved on.

You finish your meal in parallel with them—present but not connected. Safe but separate.

The conversation keeps going. You ask what class they're in. They mention something about the professor. Someone else joins in with a complaint about the homework.

You're part of it now—not the center, but included. It's messy and unscripted and more than you expected.

Your brain is already replaying the exchange. Did "not bad" sound weird? Should you have said more? Did they actually want to talk or were they just being polite?

You're eating mechanically now, more focused on the internal replay than the food in front of you.

The story keeps growing. They're definitely talking about you. The person who laughed just now—was that about you? You shouldn't have come here. You shouldn't have sat here. Everyone knows you don't belong.

The meal tastes like nothing. You're counting the seconds until you can leave.

Your phone is out. The silence passes. When you look up, someone is getting up to leave. The table dynamic has shifted.

You finish your meal behind the safety of your screen. It's not connection, but it's completion.

You stay, but you're watching everything. Every laugh feels like it might be about you. Every pause makes you want to check if you're doing something wrong.

The meal finishes. You survived it. But you're not sure if this counted as progress or just endurance.

endings.title: Present & Connected
endings.text:
You walk out. The door swings shut behind you. The noise fades.

Here's what happened: you entered a crowded space that made you uncomfortable. You sat near people. You spoke. They responded. It wasn't a breakthrough—it was just ordinary.

But ordinary is what you've been avoiding. And you just did ordinary.

You let neutral be neutral. You stayed through the hard part. You let the room be the room.

Next: Same move, one beat further into conversation.

transferPrompts.default: One follow-up question. Today. Real conversation.

byRoute.route_direct_connect: Same room, different strangers. See if it's easier the second time.

reflectionPrompts: Where else do you turn neutral into rejection before the moment proves anything?
What would change if you let more rooms be ordinary?

endings.title: Steady & Grounded
endings.text:
You're walking back. The meal is done. The interaction is behind you.

Your brain could start the replay—picking apart every word, every pause, every look. But instead, you let it settle. It happened. It was fine. You don't need to analyze it into something worse.

You did the hard thing and then you let it be done. That's the part most people miss—they do the hard thing and then replay it until it becomes a loss.

You didn't.

Next: Bolder seating choice. Same clean exit.

transferPrompts.default: After your next real interaction: two minutes, then done. No replay after.

reflectionPrompts: Where else do you turn wins into losses after the fact?
What would change if you stopped replaying and just moved on?

endings.title: Quiet But Present
endings.text:
You stayed. You ate your meal. You shared space with another person without anything going wrong.

It wasn't social. It wasn't a breakthrough. But you were there. Near another human. And you completed what you came to do.

Not every win needs to be loud. You found a step that worked—and you took it.

Next: Same approach. Catch their eye on the way out. One small upgrade.

transferPrompts.default: Sit near someone. Let proximity be the whole task. No conversation required.

reflectionPrompts: Where else do you demand the full performance when showing up would count?
What's one small upgrade from here?

endings.title: Still Here
endings.text:
You finished your meal. You stayed in the space. That's more than you might have done last week, last month, last year.

It's easy to dismiss this. You sat alone. You didn't talk to anyone. You kept your head down.

But you also didn't leave. You can be in this space without collapsing. That's data.

You met the baseline. Now you can build.

Next: Same room. One table closer.

transferPrompts.default: Public space tomorrow. Ten minutes. Just be there.

reflectionPrompts: Where else do you show up safe but wonder what happens if you moved one step closer?
What kept you there?

endings.title: Stumble, Then Steady
endings.text:
You caught yourself mid-spiral. That's harder than it sounds.

Your brain started building a story—they didn't want you there, their tone meant rejection, you should leave—and you interrupted it. You stayed anyway.

The meal wasn't comfortable. But you completed it while aware of what your brain was doing. You didn't let the spiral finish writing itself.

Spirals want to complete. You interrupted one mid-sentence.

Next: Same scenario. Catch the distortion earlier—at the moment you start writing the story, not after.

transferPrompts.default: When the story starts: 'That's a guess, not a fact.'

reflectionPrompts: Where else do you finish the rejection story before reality gets a vote?
What tipped you off that you were spiraling?

endings.title: Did It, But...
endings.text:
You stayed. You talked. You completed the meal.

And now you're replaying every moment. The way your voice sounded. The pause before they answered. Whether they looked at you weird when you left. The small thing you said that might have been awkward.

You did the hard thing. And then you turned it into evidence against yourself.

The replay is where wins go to die. You did well. The replay is lying about it.

Next: Same scenario. Stop the replay before it starts. Two minutes after the meal ends, then done.

transferPrompts.default: After your next real interaction: two minutes, then done. No replay.

reflectionPrompts: Where else do you turn wins into losses after the fact?
Is the replay giving you facts or just drafting a story?

smallestBetterMove.description: Read the response as neutral instead of negative

endings.title: Clear-Eyed
endings.text:
You're walking away. The meal is done. The interactions are behind you.

You don't feel triumphant. You also don't feel like a failure. You feel like someone who did a hard thing and is now moving on.

Not every experience needs to be labeled. Some things are just things.

You let the moment end without inflating it or deflating it. That's how you keep the win.

Next: Different table, different time of day. One more conversational beat.

transferPrompts.default: Next hard conversation: resist labeling it success or failure. Let it just be.

reflectionPrompts: What would change if more experiences just ended without a verdict?
Where else do you force a label onto something that doesn't need one?

endings.title: Still Processing
endings.text:
You're not sure what to make of it.

You stayed. That's something. But did it go well? Did it go badly? You can't quite tell. The experience sits in that uncomfortable middle zone where you don't know how to categorize it.

That uncertainty is okay. Not everything resolves neatly. You showed up, you stayed, you didn't bail.

The meaning doesn't need to arrive yet.

Next: Same scenario. See if it feels clearer the second time.

transferPrompts.default: Let one ambiguous interaction sit without forcing a verdict. 24 hours. See what happens.

reflectionPrompts: Where else do you force a verdict before the data is in?
What happens if you let something be unresolved?

endings.title: Done
endings.text:
You did what you came to do. You ate. You're leaving.

It wasn't a highlight. It wasn't a disaster. It was a meal in a dining hall, which is exactly as mundane as it sounds.

But mundane was the point. You proved you can participate in ordinary life.

Next: Same baseline. One small risk. Ask a question, sit closer, stay longer. Pick one.

transferPrompts.default: Same place tomorrow. Same task. One small upgrade.

reflectionPrompts: What's the smallest upgrade that still counts?
What made this feel manageable?

endings.title: Solitary But Present
endings.text:
You ate alone. That's not a failure—it's where you're at.

The corner table was safe. You stayed in the space. You completed the meal.

You did what you could do today. That counts.

Next: Same scenario. Try the reader table instead.

transferPrompts.default: Public space tomorrow. One seat closer than today.

reflectionPrompts: What made the corner feel necessary?
What's one step closer that still feels doable?

endings.title: What If
endings.text:
You ate alone. And now you're wondering.

What if you'd sat at the other table? What if you'd said something to someone? Would it have been better? Worse? The same?

That curiosity means part of you wanted more. Hold onto that. Use it next time.

Next: Satisfy the curiosity. Try the reader table or the group table.

transferPrompts.default: Act on the 'what if.' Try one thing you wondered about.

reflectionPrompts: What was the 'what if' you noticed?
What would it take to find out?

endings.title: The Easy Way
endings.text:
You stayed. But you also played it safe.

Your inner critic is already talking: you should have sat somewhere else. You should have talked to someone. You took the easy way out.

The critic is too harsh—but it's also pointing somewhere. There's a version of you that wanted to do more. That version is still there.

The question isn't whether you failed. You didn't. The question is whether you want a harder path next time.

Next: Same scenario. One level further on the seating choice.

transferPrompts.default: Tomorrow: one harder option than today.

reflectionPrompts: Where else do you use pressure as fuel and stall out anyway?
What's one harder option you could try next?

smallestBetterMove.description: Choose the reader table instead of sitting alone

endings.title: The Loop
endings.text:
You left. The relief was immediate. You're outside, away from the noise and the people and the feeling that everyone was watching.

But here's what avoidance does: it teaches your brain the dining hall is dangerous. That you can't handle it. Next time, entering will be harder.

Your brain just logged: 'Confirmed: too hard.'

This isn't permanent failure. It's one run. But the pattern matters. Avoidance compounds.

Next: Try again. Enter and stand for 30 seconds. No expectations beyond that.

(If you leave early, there's a hidden route: come back.)

transferPrompts.default: Tomorrow: enter, stand for 30 seconds. No expectations beyond that.

reflectionPrompts: Where else do you leave before the moment gets a vote?
What would staying one more minute have cost you?

smallestBetterMove.description: Sit at the corner table instead of leaving

endings.title: The Comeback
endings.text:
You left. And then you came back.

That second entry is the move almost nobody makes. Most people who leave stay gone. You didn't. You felt the relief of escape, and then you walked back into the discomfort on purpose.

Escape usually wins forever. You just proved it doesn't have to. Your brain logged 'I can come back' instead of 'I can't handle it.'

Next: Start with direct entry. See if you can bypass the bail-and-return phase entirely.

transferPrompts.default: If you bail this week, return within 10 minutes. That's the rep.

reflectionPrompts: Where else do you treat leaving as final when it doesn't have to be?
What made you decide to come back?

Use of grounding techniques to stay present

llmHints.scenarioContext: College student with social anxiety navigating a crowded dining hall. Core challenges: entering a crowded space, choosing where to sit (alone, near one person, near a group), interpreting ambiguous social responses accurately, tolerating awkward silences, and metabolizing the experience afterward without distorting it.
coachingFocus: Post-event processing: how they frame the experience afterward matters
Multiple valid routes to success—loud social wins aren't the only path
Distorted success: doing the hard thing but leaving feeling worse
debriefPrompts: What interpretation choices did you make during the run?
Did you notice any moment where you caught yourself catastrophizing?
How did you feel leaving compared to how the run actually went?
What would you try differently next time?
Is there a route you're curious about but haven't explored?

interpretation.whenStrong: You're reading social situations accurately. That skill transfers—use it at work, in new groups, anywhere ambiguity shows up.
interpretation.whenWeak: Your brain is adding meaning that isn't there. Practice asking: 'What's the neutral reading?'
interpretation.practiceHint: Before deciding what someone's response means, list three possible explanations.

distress_tolerance.whenStrong: You stayed through discomfort without escaping. That's real progress in building capacity.
distress_tolerance.whenWeak: You reached for a safety behavior or exit when things got hard. That's normal, but it teaches your brain you can't handle it.
distress_tolerance.practiceHint: When you want to escape, commit to staying 2 more minutes. Just 2.

directness.whenStrong: You engaged directly instead of hovering on the edges. That builds confidence.
directness.whenWeak: You stayed on the periphery. Direct engagement is the faster path to learning you can handle it.
directness.practiceHint: Try one direct action per social situation—ask a question, make a comment, sit at the table.

recovery.whenStrong: You came back from a setback. That's one of the rarest and most valuable skills.
recovery.whenWeak: When things got hard, you didn't try again. Recovery is a learnable skill.
recovery.practiceHint: If you bail from something, give yourself 10 minutes, then try again.

self_compassion.whenStrong: You're being fair to yourself about what happened. That helps you try again.
self_compassion.whenWeak: Your inner critic is loud. The harsh voice doesn't help you improve.
self_compassion.practiceHint: Ask: 'What would I say to a friend who did exactly what I did?'

interpretation_distortion.detected: You interpreted a neutral moment negatively. That's a common pattern—noticing it is the first step.
interpretation_distortion.nextStep: Before your next social interaction, predict what you'll assume. Then check if it matches reality.

avoidance_at_threshold.detected: You left right when things were about to get meaningful. This pattern keeps you stuck.
avoidance_at_threshold.nextStep: Next time you want to leave, commit to staying 3 more minutes. Just 3.

recovery_success.detected: You came back after a setback. That's rare and valuable.
recovery_success.nextStep: Trust this skill. You can recover. Use it in real life.

safety_behavior.detected: You used your phone or another shield. It felt protective but limited what you could learn.
safety_behavior.nextStep: Try the same scenario without the safety behavior. See what happens.

grounded_interpretation.detected: You read a social situation accurately. Nice work.
grounded_interpretation.nextStep: Apply this in a new context—different situation, same skill.

self_attack_spiral.detected: You're being harsh on yourself about how it went. That doesn't help.
self_attack_spiral.nextStep: Write down what actually happened without judgment. Just facts.

distress_tolerated.detected: You stayed through discomfort. That builds real capacity.
distress_tolerated.nextStep: Push slightly further next time. Same discomfort, longer duration or higher stakes.

stuckMoment.description: Standing at the entrance of a crowded dining hall, unsure where to sit or whether you can handle the social exposure
stuckMoment.trigger: Entering a crowded social space alone where seating choices signal social competence
stuckMoment.internalExperience: Heart racing, scanning for safe spots, assuming everyone is watching and judging, wanting to retreat

realWorldAnalogs: Entering a crowded coffee shop and choosing where to sit
Arriving at a party where you don't know many people
Joining a table at a work cafeteria
Walking into a gym during peak hours
Sitting in a waiting room full of strangers

patternLabelMap.mind_reading: You filled in what they were thinking
patternLabelMap.emotional_reasoning: You treated the feeling like bad news
patternLabelMap.experiential_avoidance: You left at the hardest moment
patternLabelMap.perfectionism: You needed it to be perfect first
patternLabelMap.distress_intolerance: You couldn't stay with the discomfort
patternLabelMap.recovery_success: You came back after pulling away
patternLabelMap.overcontrol: You tried to control too much
patternLabelMap.overforcing: You pushed and your system pushed back
patternLabelMap.grounded_interpretation: You read the moment for what it was
patternLabelMap.micro_step_success: You found a move small enough to work
patternLabelMap.distress_tolerated: You stayed through the hard part
patternLabelMap.direct_communication: You said what needed to be said
patternLabelMap.flexible_response: You adjusted when it didn't work
patternLabelMap.premature_exit: You protected yourself fast, but stayed stuck
patternLabelMap.post_event_processing: You replayed it until it became something worse

routeInterpretations.whatShowedUp: You entered, sat with people, read the moment accurately, and let it be ordinary.
routeInterpretations.dominantUserFacingPatternLabel: You let the room be the room
routeInterpretations.routeReinforcement: You gave your brain data it couldn't get from outside. The room wasn't dangerous. Now it knows that—not because you told it, but because you showed it.
routeInterpretations.routeNextRep: Same move, different room. Sit with strangers somewhere else.
routeInterpretations.routeWhyItMatters: The fear stays believable when you avoid. You stopped avoiding.
routeInterpretations.routeIfPatternKeepsRunning: The gap between what you expect and what actually happens keeps shrinking.
routeInterpretations.routeTransferBridge: One follow-up question. Today. Real conversation.

routeInterpretations.whatShowedUp: You chose proximity without forcing interaction. You sat near someone, completed the meal, and let that be the whole thing.
routeInterpretations.routeReinforcement: You found a move your brain could say yes to. That's not settling—that's how you expand what's possible.
routeInterpretations.routeNextRep: One table closer. That's the whole upgrade.
routeInterpretations.routeWhyItMatters: You didn't need to be charming or impressive. You just needed to show up. You did.
routeInterpretations.routeIfPatternKeepsRunning: Each time you find a workable step, the next step gets easier to see.
routeInterpretations.routeTransferBridge: Public space. One seat closer than comfortable.

routeInterpretations.whatShowedUp: You misread the tone—your brain started building rejection—and then you caught it. You stayed anyway.
routeInterpretations.dominantUserFacingPatternLabel: You caught the story before it finished writing itself
routeInterpretations.routeReinforcement: Spirals want to complete. You interrupted one mid-sentence. That's harder than never starting.
routeInterpretations.routeNextRep: Catch it earlier. Name the story before it locks in.
routeInterpretations.routeWhyItMatters: You don't have to believe every draft your brain writes.
routeInterpretations.routeIfPatternKeepsRunning: The spiral gets shorter each time you interrupt it.
routeInterpretations.routeTransferBridge: Notice when you're writing a story. Don't finish it.

routeInterpretations.whatShowedUp: You left. And then you came back. That second entry is the move almost nobody makes.
routeInterpretations.dominantUserFacingPatternLabel: Leaving didn't have to be permanent
routeInterpretations.routeReinforcement: Escape usually wins forever. You just proved it doesn't have to. Your brain logged 'I can come back' instead of 'I can't handle it.'
routeInterpretations.routeNextRep: If you bail this week, return within 10 minutes. That's the rep.
routeInterpretations.routeWhyItMatters: Most people who leave stay gone. You didn't.
routeInterpretations.routeIfPatternKeepsRunning: Escape becomes a pause, not a verdict.
routeInterpretations.routeTransferBridge: Next time you bail, give yourself permission to go back.

routeInterpretations.whatShowedUp: You stayed in the space. You ate your meal. You didn't leave.
routeInterpretations.routeReinforcement: The corner is still in the room. You didn't need to connect to count. You just needed to be there. You were.
routeInterpretations.routeWhyItMatters: You met the baseline. Now you can build.
routeInterpretations.routeIfPatternKeepsRunning: The corner gets less necessary. The room gets less charged.
routeInterpretations.routeTransferBridge: Public space tomorrow. Ten minutes. Just be there.

routeInterpretations.whatShowedUp: You did the hard thing—you sat with people. But then you turned their flat face into proof they didn't want you there.
routeInterpretations.dominantUserFacingPatternLabel: You filled in the blank with rejection
routeInterpretations.routeReinforcement: Their face was neutral. You made it hostile. Now your brain treats the story you wrote as evidence. That's the trap.
routeInterpretations.routeNextRep: Before deciding what their face meant, ask: What's the boring explanation?
routeInterpretations.routeWhyItMatters: You're not reading their mind—you're projecting yours.
routeInterpretations.routeIfPatternKeepsRunning: Every blank face becomes a verdict. The world gets smaller.
routeInterpretations.routeTransferBridge: After your next ambiguous interaction, wait 60 seconds before deciding what it meant.

routeInterpretations.whatShowedUp: You stayed. You talked. And now you're replaying every moment, looking for what went wrong.
routeInterpretations.routeReinforcement: You can do the hard thing and still turn it into evidence against yourself. The replay is where wins go to die.
routeInterpretations.routeNextRep: After your next real interaction, two minutes max. Then: 'Done.'
routeInterpretations.routeWhyItMatters: You did well. The replay lied about it.
routeInterpretations.routeIfPatternKeepsRunning: Every interaction becomes a test you probably failed. Even the ones that went fine.
routeInterpretations.routeTransferBridge: Notice when the replay starts. Label it. Redirect.

stepInterpretations.userFacingPatternLabel: You didn't wait to feel ready
stepInterpretations.whatShowedUp: You entered when your system wanted to hesitate.
stepInterpretations.functionalIntent: Your body wanted more time. You overrode it.
stepInterpretations.immediatePayoff: You're in. The decision is made. No more hovering.
stepInterpretations.reinforcement: Your brain just logged: 'I can enter without waiting for permission from myself.'
stepInterpretations.tryNext: Enter one space 30 seconds faster than feels comfortable.
stepInterpretations.whyThisMatters: The hesitation at the door is where most people get stuck.
stepInterpretations.consequenceIfRepeated: Each direct entry makes the door less significant.

stepInterpretations.whatShowedUp: The phone became a shield between you and the room.
stepInterpretations.cost: The phone says: 'This room requires protection.'
stepInterpretations.reinforcement: Your brain just logged: 'See, I needed it.' The space stays dangerous because you never let it prove otherwise.
stepInterpretations.tryNext: Phone stays in pocket for the first 2 minutes.
stepInterpretations.whyThisMatters: Every time you use it, you confirm the threat.
stepInterpretations.consequenceIfRepeated: The phone becomes required. You feel naked without it.

stepInterpretations.userFacingPatternLabel: You left before the room got a vote
stepInterpretations.whatShowedUp: The door was right there. You turned around.
stepInterpretations.functionalIntent: You wanted to skip finding out.
stepInterpretations.cost: Your brain just logged: 'Confirmed: too hard.' Next time starts harder.
stepInterpretations.reinforcement: Avoidance compounds. Each exit teaches your brain the space is dangerous.
stepInterpretations.tryNext: Tomorrow: enter, stand inside for 30 seconds. No expectations.
stepInterpretations.whyThisMatters: The hardest part is entering. You left before testing that.
stepInterpretations.consequenceIfRepeated: The dining hall becomes a place you 'can't go.' Your world shrinks.

stepInterpretations.whatYouChose: You sat at the group table.
stepInterpretations.functionalIntent: Part of you wanted the corner. You went the other way.
stepInterpretations.immediatePayoff: You're in the game. The decision is irreversible.
stepInterpretations.cost: Your nervous system is lit up. Stakes feel higher.
stepInterpretations.reinforcement: Your brain just logged: 'I can approach, not just observe.'
stepInterpretations.tryNext: Next time, ask one question after sitting down.
stepInterpretations.whyThisMatters: You went toward the thing your brain said to avoid.
stepInterpretations.consequenceIfRepeated: Approaching gets easier. The group table becomes ordinary.

stepInterpretations.userFacingPatternLabel: You stayed, but behind a buffer
stepInterpretations.whatShowedUp: The corner table. Safe. Separate. Still in the room.
stepInterpretations.functionalIntent: You wanted distance from the social pressure.
stepInterpretations.immediatePayoff: You're in the space but protected.
stepInterpretations.cost: You didn't test what happens at the harder option.
stepInterpretations.reinforcement: The corner lets you say 'I went.' But the harder tables stay untested.
stepInterpretations.whyThisMatters: There's a difference between showing up and arriving.
stepInterpretations.consequenceIfRepeated: The corner becomes your default. The rest of the room stays dangerous.

stepInterpretations.whatYouChose: You read their tone as just... neutral.
stepInterpretations.whatShowedUp: Their response was flat. And you let it stay flat.
stepInterpretations.functionalIntent: Your brain wanted to find a signal. You chose not to invent one.
stepInterpretations.immediatePayoff: The moment didn't spiral. You stayed grounded.
stepInterpretations.reinforcement: Your brain just logged: 'Not everything means something. Sometimes people are just there.'
stepInterpretations.tryNext: Next ambiguous moment, ask: What's the boring explanation?
stepInterpretations.consequenceIfRepeated: If you keep reading moments accurately, the default assumption shifts from threat to neutral.

stepInterpretations.userFacingPatternLabel: You wrote rejection onto a blank face
stepInterpretations.whatYouChose: You decided they didn't want you there.
stepInterpretations.whatShowedUp: Their tone was flat. Your brain said: 'They don't want you here.'
stepInterpretations.functionalIntent: Your brain was scanning for threat. It invented one.
stepInterpretations.immediatePayoff: The story makes sense. Your fear feels justified.
stepInterpretations.cost: You just poisoned a neutral moment.
stepInterpretations.reinforcement: Your brain just logged: ambiguity = danger.
stepInterpretations.tryNext: Next flat face, wait 60 seconds before deciding what it meant.
stepInterpretations.whyThisMatters: You're not reading their mind—you're projecting yours.
stepInterpretations.consequenceIfRepeated: Every flat tone becomes rejection. Your world gets smaller.

stepInterpretations.whatShowedUp: Your brain was building a rejection story. You noticed—and stopped.
stepInterpretations.functionalIntent: The spiral wanted to run. You interrupted it.
stepInterpretations.immediatePayoff: You're still here. The moment didn't collapse.
stepInterpretations.cost: The discomfort didn't disappear—you sat with it.
stepInterpretations.reinforcement: Your brain just logged: 'Spirals are interruptible.'
stepInterpretations.tryNext: When the story starts, say: 'That's a guess, not a fact.'
stepInterpretations.whyThisMatters: You interrupted a story before it finished writing itself.
stepInterpretations.consequenceIfRepeated: Spirals get shorter each time you catch them.

stepInterpretations.whatShowedUp: There was a lull. You could have let it pass. You didn't.
stepInterpretations.functionalIntent: Part of you wanted to wait. You went first.
stepInterpretations.immediatePayoff: You're in the conversation now. The passive moment became active.
stepInterpretations.cost: Higher stakes. More to potentially replay later.
stepInterpretations.reinforcement: Your brain just logged: 'I can initiate, not just respond.'
stepInterpretations.tryNext: One follow-up question. Today. Real conversation.
stepInterpretations.whyThisMatters: You went first. Most people don't.
stepInterpretations.consequenceIfRepeated: Speaking up gets easier. Silence becomes optional.

stepInterpretations.userFacingPatternLabel: You stayed through the awkward part
stepInterpretations.whatShowedUp: The silence was uncomfortable. You let it be uncomfortable.
stepInterpretations.functionalIntent: You wanted to fill it, escape it, fix it. You did nothing.
stepInterpretations.immediatePayoff: The moment passed. You're still here.
stepInterpretations.cost: The discomfort wasn't avoided—it was felt.
stepInterpretations.reinforcement: Your brain just logged: 'Awkward silences are survivable.'
stepInterpretations.tryNext: Next awkward moment, let 5 seconds pass before acting.
stepInterpretations.whyThisMatters: You can't engage if you can't stay. You stayed.
stepInterpretations.consequenceIfRepeated: Silence becomes less threatening. You outlast what others flee.

stepInterpretations.whatShowedUp: You left. And then you walked back in.
stepInterpretations.functionalIntent: The relief of escape wasn't enough. You wanted more than safety.
stepInterpretations.cost: Re-entering is harder than entering. You did it anyway.
stepInterpretations.reinforcement: Your brain just logged: 'Setbacks are temporary. Escape isn't final.'
stepInterpretations.tryNext: If you bail this week, return within 10 minutes.
stepInterpretations.whyThisMatters: Most people who leave stay gone. You didn't.
stepInterpretations.consequenceIfRepeated: Leaving becomes a pause, not a verdict.

stepInterpretations.whatYouChose: You started analyzing what went wrong.
stepInterpretations.whatShowedUp: The experience was over. Then you started picking it apart.
stepInterpretations.functionalIntent: Your brain started scanning for what went wrong.
stepInterpretations.immediatePayoff: It feels productive—like you're learning something.
stepInterpretations.cost: The replay turns a neutral moment into evidence against yourself.
stepInterpretations.reinforcement: Your brain just logged: 'Every interaction needs post-analysis.' It doesn't.
stepInterpretations.tryNext: Next social moment: two minutes, then done. No replay after.
stepInterpretations.whyThisMatters: The replay is where wins go to die.
stepInterpretations.consequenceIfRepeated: Every interaction becomes a test you probably failed.

stepInterpretations.userFacingPatternLabel: You let the win stay a win
stepInterpretations.whatShowedUp: The experience ended. You let it settle without picking it apart.
stepInterpretations.functionalIntent: Your brain could have started the replay. You didn't let it.
stepInterpretations.immediatePayoff: The win stays a win. No second-guessing.
stepInterpretations.reinforcement: Your brain just logged: 'Experiences can end without analysis.'
stepInterpretations.tryNext: Next hard conversation, resist labeling it success or failure. Let it just be.
stepInterpretations.whyThisMatters: How you interpret afterward matters as much as what happened.
stepInterpretations.consequenceIfRepeated: Social moments become data, not trials. You stop draining wins.

routeLevel.whatShowedUp: You took a path that didn't fit a mapped route.
routeLevel.reinforcement: Your path was unique. What matters: did you stay, or did you bail?
routeLevel.whyItMatters: Pay attention to where you felt the pull to leave or stay.
routeLevel.ifPatternKeepsRunning: You'll find the routes that fit as you run it again.

routeLevel.whatShowedUp: You moved through a hard moment. That counts.
routeLevel.reinforcement: Every run gives your brain data. Even the messy ones.

stepLevel.functionalIntent: Your brain was managing the moment.
stepLevel.cost: There may have been a different path.
stepLevel.reinforcement: Each choice gives your brain data about what's possible.
stepLevel.tryNext: Notice what you felt here. Try something different next time.
stepLevel.whyThisMatters: You're building awareness of the pattern.

insightBeats.insightText: You grabbed armor before anyone fired a shot. Your system traded 'find out if it's safe' for 'assume it's not.'
insightBeats.whyItMatters: Every time the phone goes up, your brain logs: 'See? You needed it.' The space stays dangerous because you never let it prove otherwise.
insightBeats.tryNextCue: Pocket stays closed for 90 seconds after you enter.

microInterventions.text: Put it in your pocket. Leave it there for one minute.
microInterventions.why: You break the reflex by not completing it.

microInterventions.text: Set it face-down on the table. Hands off.
microInterventions.why: Present but not protecting. Halfway honest.

insightBeats.insightText: Their face gave you nothing. You wrote 'rejection' anyway. You made that up.
insightBeats.whyItMatters: Flat face. You filled it in. Now the blank is 'proof.'
insightBeats.tryNextCue: Ask: what's the most boring explanation for their face?

microInterventions.text: Silently say: 'Or they're just tired.'
microInterventions.why: The boring explanation is almost always the true one.

microInterventions.text: Label it out loud: 'That was a guess.'
microInterventions.why: Calling it a guess breaks its authority.

microInterventions.text: Don't decide yet. Give it 60 seconds.
microInterventions.why: The spiral needs you to conclude fast. Don't.

insightBeats.insightText: Your system said 'not that table' and you went anyway. That override is the whole skill.
insightBeats.whyItMatters: Fear shrinks when you approach what it says to avoid. You just gave your brain data it couldn't get from the corner.

microInterventions.text: You're here. Don't bolt. Let the discomfort settle.
microInterventions.why: Staying through the spike is what changes it.

microInterventions.text: Say one sentence. Anything. The content doesn't matter.
microInterventions.why: Action solidifies approach. Words are secondary.

insightBeats.insightText: You left. And then you walked back in. That second entry is the move almost nobody makes.
insightBeats.whyItMatters: Escape usually wins permanently. You just proved it doesn't have to. Your brain logged 'I can come back' instead of 'I can't handle it.'

microInterventions.text: You're back. That's the win. Nothing else required.
microInterventions.why: Don't add goals. The return is complete.

microInterventions.text: One small thing: sit down, order, look around. Pick one.
microInterventions.why: Low bar protects the recovery.

insightBeats.insightText: You were writing a rejection script and you stopped typing. That interrupt is harder than never starting.
insightBeats.whyItMatters: The spiral wanted you to finish the story. You refused. That's not nothing—that's the skill working in real time.

microInterventions.text: Don't conclude. Hold the not-knowing for 30 seconds.
microInterventions.why: Uncertainty is tolerable. You don't have to resolve it.

microInterventions.text: Stay until the spike passes. Don't leave at peak.
microInterventions.why: Leaving now teaches your brain the peak is unmanageable.

microInterventions.text: Look at them again. Check if the data matches your story.
microInterventions.why: Second look often contradicts first read.

insightBeats.insightText: You stayed, but in a way that kept the room from really happening to you. That's showing up without arriving.
insightBeats.whyItMatters: The corner lets you say 'I went.' But your brain still logged 'too risky to really join.' The fear stays intact.
insightBeats.tryNextCue: Same room. One table closer. Let the hiding place get worse.

microInterventions.text: Look at the group for 5 seconds. No smile. Just look.
microInterventions.why: Looking is half the distance to sitting there.

microInterventions.text: Count who's actually looking at you. It's almost always zero.
microInterventions.why: The spotlight feeling lies. Check it.

microInterventions.text: Finish the meal here. Don't leave early, even from the corner.
microInterventions.why: Early exit erases partial credit.

insightBeats.insightText: You got close enough to feel it—and then you bailed. Your brain just filed 'dining hall' under 'confirmed threat.'
insightBeats.whyItMatters: Escape feels like relief. Your body just logged the peak as 'too much to stay.' Next time starts harder.
insightBeats.tryNextCue: 30 seconds inside. Stand there. That's the whole task.

microInterventions.text: One step back in. That's it. No further goal.
microInterventions.why: Tiny reversal breaks the escape momentum.

microInterventions.text: Shrink the goal: 30 seconds inside, then you can leave.
microInterventions.why: The bar was too high. Lower it to survivable.

microInterventions.text: Say: 'This is the collapse moment.' Don't act on it yet.
microInterventions.why: Naming creates a gap between urge and action.

insightBeats.insightText: Your system scanned for threat and you didn't take the bait. You let neutral be neutral.
insightBeats.whyItMatters: This is what recalibration looks like. One accurate read at a time, the threat detector gets retrained.

microInterventions.text: Mark it: 'Neutral face. I didn't add a story.'
microInterventions.why: Explicit logging strengthens the accurate pattern.

microInterventions.text: Stay a few minutes longer. Extend the data.
microInterventions.why: Duration at accurate interpretation compounds the learning.
